newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FEATURE-Internet in Asia offers own business plan.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Internet in Asia offers own business plan.

text.p: From Jawi-script Internet Web pages to electronic shopping malls featuring local goods, corporations are nudging into Asia with business products and solutions tailored for the region.

Despite the recent gloomy observation of a U.S. software executive that the Internet has so far been unprofitable for businesses, the prospect of cyberspace cash is luring a string of products in one of the world's fastest-growing markets.
A report from the International Data Corporation (IDC) says that Asia-Pacific will surpass Europe as the world's second largest information technology market after the United States by the year 2000.
By the year 2010, China will topple the U.S. as the world's biggest IT market, IDC predicts.
USE OF INTERNET FOR SALES GAINING

Use of the Internet to sell products and services is catching hold in the region, prompting the formation in May of the Asian Pacific Internet Association (APIA), which aims to promote the business interests of the Internet-related industry.

"There was no organisation that focused on business issues, on this region, and on Internet," said Roger Hicks, a member of APIA's steering committee from New Zealand, who attended the Internet Society's annual conference here in June.
The group's other steering members come from Korea, Japan, Malaysia, Hong Kong, Singapore and China.

One of APIA's aims is to challenge Internet tariffs, which it believes imposes unfair costs to regional Internet Service Providers as the communications lines often have to be routed to the United States -- where most of the world's Internet sites are based -- before coming back to Asia.
REGION-SPECIFIC PRODUCTS EMERGE
Several companies are responding to the clarion call of finding region-specific products and services.
Montreal-based Alis Technologis Inc announced near the end of June that it would develop Internet products based on the Arabic-related Jawi script used for the Malay language.
Jawi was the original script for the Malay language used in Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei. The project's officials estimate over 200 million people use Jawi.
Even the older folk of rural Malay villages "can use the computer to get information", said Mashkuri Yaacob, chairman of Jawinet, a Malaysian non-profit organisation that promotes the Jawi script.
CYBERSHOPPING DEBUTS IN MALAYSIA

Online shopping, which has already emerged in other countries, made its debut in Malaysia at the sidelines of the Internet Society's seventh annual conference. The non-profit group is the key organisation for development of the Internet.
Malaysia Internet access provider Jaring began its Mall of Malaysia (http://www.mom.com.my) in June with a half-dozen stores offering goods ranging from toothpaste to comics.
It will even eventually feature a local farm that sells organically-grown produce in cyberspace, said Tengku Azzman Shariffadeen, chief executive officer of Internet service provider MIMOS Bhd.
Malaysia's population of about 20 million has over 100,000 Internet users. "The kind of customer we are targeting are Net surfers," Tengku Azzman said.
For now, buyers can only use Mastercard to pay for purchases. Encryption of the payment document where the credit card number is entered ensures privacy.
ASIAN-BASED WEB SEARCHES POSSIBLE
The need for Asian-based information at faster speeds on the Net is behind Malaysian firm Alam Teknokrat Sdn Bhd's tie-up with U.S. company AltaVista Internet Software Inc ALTV.O.
Alam Teknokrat has set up outside Kuala Lumpur an Internet search "mirror site" (http://altavista.skali.com.my) that duplicates AltaVista's main search facility at Palo Alto, California.
As part of the service, Alam Teknokrat is also providing news from Malaysia's government-owned news agency Bernama.
The use of the Asian-based mirror site will allow for quicker Web page searches, as the cyberspace queries will be routed within Asia rather than sent to the United States.

"This service will provide dramatic performance advantages to millions of Internet users in Asia," Alam Teknokrat said in a statement. It said 150,000 search requests per day from Asia were currently being handled by AltaVista in the United States.
PROBLEM OF NON-ENGLISH SPEAKERS
"A lot of the issues on Internet are English-based," said Hicks of APIA. "I've heard there's apathy in Asia-Pacific (about Internet issues), but it's very difficult to answer in a foreign language."

He said one thrust of his group was to make the Internet more widely-available within Asia-Pacific. "We believe it's very important to bring the less developed ones (countries)" to the group, he said.
